title: Green hydrogen and grey hydrogen compared

figure.name: x-compare
figure.verdict: Same gas, very different carbon footprint

explain.say: Hydrogen is clean to use, because burning it or using it in a fuel cell makes only water. But how it is made matters. Green hydrogen is made by splitting water into hydrogen and oxygen using electricity from wind or solar power.

draw.text: Green hydrogen and grey hydrogen compared

draw.name: x-compare
draw.verdict: Same gas, very different carbon footprint

explain.say: Grey hydrogen, by far the most common today, is made by reacting natural gas with very hot steam. It is cheaper, but it releases about 10 kilograms of carbon dioxide for every kilogram of hydrogen.

draw.name: x-compare
draw.verdict: Same gas, very different carbon footprint

explain.say: Splitting water, called electrolysis, loses energy: roughly 70 percent of the electricity ends up stored in the hydrogen and the rest becomes heat. So hydrogen is best used where batteries struggle, like steelmaking and fertiliser.

There is also blue hydrogen, made from gas like grey hydrogen but with the carbon dioxide captured and stored underground. Green hydrogen costs more today, but gets cheaper as wind and solar power do.

faq.a: In an electrolyser, electricity passes through water and splits it into hydrogen at one electrode and oxygen at the other. If the electricity comes from wind, solar or hydro, no carbon dioxide is released.
By steam methane reforming: natural gas and steam react at around 700 to 1,000 degrees Celsius over a catalyst, making hydrogen and carbon dioxide. The carbon dioxide is released into the air.
asks: How is hydrogen made from natural gas?

faq.a: Blue hydrogen is made from natural gas like grey hydrogen, but most of the carbon dioxide is captured and stored deep underground instead of being released.
asks: What do the hydrogen colours mean?

faq.a: Electrolysers store roughly 60 to 80 percent of the electricity's energy in the hydrogen. Turning it back into electricity in a fuel cell loses about half again, so only around a third comes back overall.
asks: Is hydrogen a waste of electricity?

faq.q: What is hydrogen used for today?
faq.a: Mostly to make ammonia for fertiliser and to refine oil. In future, clean hydrogen could make steel without coal, fuel ships and store energy for weeks.

facts: Most hydrogen produced today is made from natural gas or coal, with only a small share made by electrolysis.
Making one kilogram of hydrogen from natural gas releases roughly 9 to 12 kilograms of carbon dioxide.
